```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_survival <- requireNamespace("survival", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5, dpi = 96,
                      eval = has_survival)
```

This vignette follows a complete analysis of a single event: description, comparison of groups,
Cox regression and its extensions, model checking and prediction. It uses two classic data sets
of the **survival** package: `lung` (advanced lung cancer, North Central Cancer Treatment Group)
and `veteran` (Veterans' Administration lung cancer trial).

```{r}
library(SurvX)
lung <- survival::lung
lung$status <- lung$status - 1                      # 0 = censored, 1 = died
lung$sex <- factor(lung$sex, 1:2, c("male", "female"))
lung$years <- lung$time / 365.25
nrow(lung); table(lung$status)
```

## 1. Describing survival: Kaplan-Meier

```{r}
k <- km(Event(years, status) ~ sex, lung)
k
summary(k, times = c(0.5, 1, 2))
```

The print gives the number of patients and deaths, the **median survival** with its confidence
interval (Brookmeyer and Crowley) and the log-rank test. Women lived longer: median
`r round(k@counts$median[k@counts$group == "female"], 2)` versus
`r round(k@counts$median[k@counts$group == "male"], 2)` years.

```{r km-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(k, median = TRUE, conf.int = TRUE)
```

The table under the plot shows the numbers at risk; the curves become uncertain where few
patients remain.

## 2. Comparing groups

`km()` already reports the log-rank test. `logrank_test()` also gives the Peto-Peto test, which
weights early differences more, and the stratified test:

```{r}
logrank_test(lung$years, lung$status, lung$sex)
logrank_test(lung$years, lung$status, lung$sex, rho = 1)
```

The restricted mean survival time (RMST) is an effect measure in time units that needs no
proportional hazards. Over the first two years:

```{r}
r_f <- rmst(lung$years[lung$sex == "female"], lung$status[lung$sex == "female"], tau = 2)
r_m <- rmst(lung$years[lung$sex == "male"], lung$status[lung$sex == "male"], tau = 2)
d <- r_f[["rmst"]] - r_m[["rmst"]]; se <- sqrt(r_f[["se"]]^2 + r_m[["se"]]^2)
round(c(female = r_f[["rmst"]], male = r_m[["rmst"]], difference = d,
        lower = d - 1.96 * se, upper = d + 1.96 * se), 3)
```

On average, women lived `r round(d, 2)` years (`r round(12 * d, 1)` months) longer during the
first two years.

## 3. Cox regression

```{r}
fit <- cox(Event(years, status) ~ sex + age + ph.ecog, lung)
fit
```

Rows with a missing covariate are removed (see the number of subjects). Each hazard ratio is
read with the other covariates held fixed: women had a
`r round(100 * (1 - exp(coef(fit)[["sexfemale"]])))`% lower death rate than men of the same age
and performance status (HR `r round(exp(coef(fit)[["sexfemale"]]), 2)`). The `Reading:` lines say
the same in words.

Ties are handled with the Efron method by default, as in `survival::coxph`; `ties = "breslow"`
gives the Breslow approximation.

### Strata

A variable whose effect is not of interest, or that violates proportional hazards, can define
strata: each stratum gets its own baseline hazard and the variable gets no coefficient.

```{r}
cox(Event(years, status) ~ sex + age + strata(ph.ecog), lung)
```

### Clustered data and robust standard errors

When rows are not independent (several rows per patient, patients within centres), `cluster()`
gives the robust variance of Lin and Wei (1989). Here, as an illustration, patients are clustered
by institution:

```{r}
cox(Event(years, status) ~ sex + age + ph.ecog + cluster(inst), lung)
```

### Delayed entry and time-varying covariates

With `Event(time, status, entry = entry)` a subject enters the risk set at `entry`. The same form
handles covariates that change over follow-up, with one row per period `(start, stop]`, as in
`survival::coxph(Surv(start, stop, event) ~ ...)`.

## 4. Checking proportional hazards

```{r}
ph_test(fit)
```

Look at the p-values of the covariates and of the global test, and at the plots for any covariate
in doubt. The veteran data give a classic example of a changing effect: that of the Karnofsky
performance score fades over time.

```{r}
vet <- survival::veteran
fv <- cox(Event(time, status) ~ trt + celltype + karno, vet)
pt <- ph_test(fv)
pt
```

```{r zph-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(pt, var = "karno")
```

The coefficient of `karno` is negative (a higher score, a lower death rate), and the smooth
rises toward zero: the protective effect is strong early and weakens later.

## 5. Time-varying effects with `tt()`

The effect of `karno` can be allowed to change with log time:

```{r}
ft <- cox(Event(time, status) ~ trt + celltype + karno + tt(karno), vet,
          tt = function(t) log(t + 20))
ft
tt_effect(ft, times = c(30, 90, 180, 365))
```

The hazard ratio per point of the score moves toward 1 as time passes. `tt_effect()` gives these
values, with confidence intervals, at any times; they are what to report.

### Choosing the form with `time_effects()`

Above, the form `log(t + 20)` was chosen by hand. `time_effects()` does the whole sequence for every
covariate: the test of a constant effect (with Holm's adjustment for the number of covariates), a
comparison of forms for the covariates that fail it (log-linear, a step at a change point chosen from
the data, a spline in log time, or functions you supply) by AIC and likelihood ratio tests, the final
model with the chosen forms, and the hazard ratio over time.

```{r}
te <- time_effects(fv, times = c(30, 90, 180, 365))
te
```

```{r te-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(te)
```

The figure shows the chosen form with its confidence band, the constant (proportional hazards)
fit as a dashed line and the scaled Schoenfeld residuals. `fix = list(karno = "piecewise")` imposes a
form, for a pre-specified analysis or a sensitivity analysis. The forms are chosen from the same data,
so the intervals of the final model are somewhat too narrow; `bootstrap = 200` repeats the whole
procedure in bootstrap samples, giving intervals that include the choice and the share of samples in
which each form is chosen. `predict(te, newdata, times)` gives survival probabilities with the
time-varying effects, and `report(te, file)` writes the analysis, with methods and references, to an
HTML file.

## 6. Residuals and functional form

Martingale residuals of a model *without* a numeric covariate, plotted against it, show the form
the covariate should take:

```{r mart, fig.height = 4}
l2 <- na.omit(lung[, c("years", "status", "sex", "age", "ph.ecog", "wt.loss")])
f0 <- cox(Event(years, status) ~ sex + ph.ecog, l2)
plot(l2$age, residuals(f0), xlab = "age", ylab = "martingale residual", col = "grey50")
lines(stats::lowess(l2$age, residuals(f0)), lwd = 2)
```

A roughly straight line supports a linear term for age. Deviance residuals point to poorly fitted
patients, and `dist_plot(fit)` checks the overall fit with Cox-Snell residuals.

## 7. Absolute predictions

```{r}
nd <- data.frame(sex = c("male", "female"), age = 65, ph.ecog = 1)
round(predict(fit, nd, times = c(0.5, 1, 2), type = "survival"), 3)
```

```{r pred-plot}
plot(fit, nd, labels = c("male, 65, ECOG 1", "female, 65, ECOG 1"))
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
p1 <- predict(fit, nd, times = 1, type = "survival")[, 1]
```

A 65-year-old woman with ECOG 1 has an estimated one-year survival of `r round(100 * p1[2])`%, a man
with the same profile `r round(100 * p1[1])`%.

## 8. Adjusted absolute risks

Hazard ratios do not say how much the *risk* would change. `adjusted_risk()` answers "what would the
risk have been had everyone received this treatment?", standardising a fitted model over the
covariates of the data (the g-formula) or weighting by the inverse probability of treatment, with
bootstrap intervals in which the models are refitted.

```{r}
fl <- cox(Event(years, status) ~ sex + age + ph.ecog, data = lung)
ar <- adjusted_risk(fl, lung, "sex", times = c(0.5, 1), method = "both", B = 0)
ar
```

```{r ar-plot, fig.height = 4}
plot(ar)
```

The two methods rest on different models (the outcome model and a model of sex given age and
performance status) and agree closely. Use `B = 200` or more for intervals; `report(ar, file)`
writes the analysis to an HTML file.

## 9. Predictive performance

`brier_score()` and `auc_t()` assess predicted risks at a horizon; `cv_compare()` compares models
by cross-validation:

```{r}
f1 <- cox(Event(years, status) ~ sex + age + ph.ecog, l2)
risk <- 1 - predict(f1, l2, times = 1, type = "survival")[, 1]
bs <- brier_score(l2$years, l2$status, risk, t = 1)
bs
auc_t(l2$years, l2$status, risk, t = 1)
```

The IPA (index of prediction accuracy) of `r round(bs[["ipa"]], 2)` means that the model removes
`r round(100 * bs[["ipa"]])`% of the prediction error of a model without covariates. These are
apparent measures, computed on the data used for fitting; `cv_compare()` gives cross-validated
ones.

## 10. Interval-censored data

When the event is found at a visit (a scan, a test, a survey wave), its time is only known to lie
between the last visit without it and the first visit with it. `Interval(left, right)` records
this: `right = Inf` for subjects without the event, `left = 0` when the event was already there at
the first visit, `left = right` for exact times. Imputing the midpoint or the right end point and
then using methods for exact times biases the estimates (Lindsey and Ryan 1998).

```{r ic-data}
set.seed(11)
n <- 300
trt <- factor(rep(c("control", "treated"), length.out = n))
age <- rnorm(n)
t <- rweibull(n, 1.4, exp(2 + 0.4 * (trt == "treated") - 0.3 * age))
visits <- t(replicate(n, cumsum(runif(8, 1, 3))))      # irregular visits
ic <- data.frame(trt, age,
                 left = sapply(seq_len(n), function(i) max(c(0, visits[i, visits[i, ] < t[i]]))),
                 right = sapply(seq_len(n), function(i) { v <- visits[i, visits[i, ] >= t[i]]; if (length(v)) min(v) else Inf }))
head(with(ic, Interval(left, right)))
```

The Turnbull estimate is the non-parametric curve for these data (the Kaplan-Meier estimate when
all times are exact); the test compares the groups with logrank scores for interval-censored data:

```{r ic-turnbull, fig.height = 4}
tb <- turnbull(Interval(left, right) ~ trt, data = ic, B = 50)
tb
plot(tb)
```

Parametric regression uses the probability of each interval, $S(L) - S(R)$, for every family; the
plot draws the Turnbull estimate for comparison:

```{r ic-parsurv, fig.height = 4}
fw <- parsurv(Interval(left, right) ~ trt + age, data = ic, baseline = "weibull", scale = "AFT")
fw
plot(fw)
```

With competing risks and a known type of event, `directcif(Interval(left, right, cause = cause) ~ x)`
fits the direct models for the cumulative incidence with $F_k(R) - F_k(L)$ (see the competing
risks vignette).

  457-481.
* Cox DR (1972). Regression models and life-tables. *JRSS B*, 34, 187-220.
* Lin DY, Wei LJ (1989). The robust inference for the Cox proportional hazards model. *JASA*, 84,
  1074-1078.
* Grambsch PM, Therneau TM (1994). Proportional hazards tests and diagnostics based on weighted
  residuals. *Biometrika*, 81, 515-526.
* Therneau TM, Grambsch PM (2000). *Modeling Survival Data: Extending the Cox Model*. Springer.
* Holm S (1979). A simple sequentially rejective multiple test procedure. *Scandinavian Journal of
  Statistics*, 6, 65-70.
* Hess KR (1994). Assessing time-by-covariate interactions in proportional hazards regression models
  using cubic spline functions. *Statistics in Medicine*, 13, 1045-1062.
* Robins J (1986). A new approach to causal inference in mortality studies with a sustained exposure
  period. *Mathematical Modelling*, 7, 1393-1512.
* Cole SR, Hernan MA (2004). Adjusted survival curves with inverse probability weights. *Computer
  Methods and Programs in Biomedicine*, 75, 45-49.
* Turnbull BW (1976). The empirical distribution function with arbitrarily grouped, censored and
  truncated data. *JRSS B*, 38, 290-295.
